title: Feelings and reactions
cando: say how things are and how they make you feel

about.text: In this lesson you talk about how things were and how they made you feel. You learn the difference between boring and bored. You read a notice board and two references, and you write a short review.
goals: Ask and answer: What was it like? It was amazing. I was so bored.
Use -ing and -ed words: confusing and confused.
Say how much with quite, too and not … enough.
Use good at, interested in and afraid of.
Review a film, a course or a day out, and say if you recommend it.

chapters.title: Did they like it?
chapters.text:
In this lesson you talk about feelings.
First, you listen to two colleagues, Priya and Kwame. It is Monday morning at work.
Priya went on a photography course. Kwame asks: What was it like? Priya says: It was amazing.
She was nervous at first, but everybody was friendly.
Then Kwame talks about a film. He says: It was so boring!
Listen to the long words. Each one has one strong part. Say that part louder.

chapters.title: boring or bored
chapters.text:
Some words have two forms. The film was boring. I was bored.
The -ing word tells you about the thing. The -ed word tells you how a person feels.
So do not say: I was boring. That means other people were bored with you!
Some words always have a small word after them. Good at. Interested in. Afraid of.
Then you say how much. Quite good means good, but not very good.
Too long means it was a problem. Not big enough means it was too small.

chapters.title: A notice board and two references
chapters.text:
Next, you read a notice board at a library. It shows free sessions, and what people said about them.
Then you read two references for the same man, Omar. One reference is long and warm. The other is very short.
Which one helps Omar more? Look for the words about him: honest, reliable, calm and hard-working.
Then you write a short review of a film, a course or a place.

chapters.title: Would you recommend it?
chapters.text:
In the task, a colleague wants to do something nice at the weekend.
Tell her about a film, a course or a day out. What was it like? How did you feel?
Say one good thing and one problem.
Say how much, too. It was quite busy. The café was too crowded.
Then say if you recommend it. Yes, it's worth it. Or: No, I wouldn't recommend it.

chapters.title: The book
chapters.text:
Last, you read a story about feelings.
Read it once for the story. Then read it again and answer the questions.

warmup.prompt: A friend asks about a film you saw. What do you talk about first?
warmup.note: There is no wrong answer. People often start with one word: amazing, boring, frightening. Then they say why.

conversation.title: What was it like?
conversation.setting: It is Monday morning. Priya and Kwame work in the same office. They are at the coffee machine.
lines: Morning, Priya! How was your weekend?
Great, thanks. I went on a photography course on Saturday.
Oh, nice! What was it like?
It was amazing. I was nervous at first, but everybody was very friendly.
The camera was quite confusing. It has too many buttons! But I learned a lot.
I'm interested in photography too. Is the course good for beginners?
Yes, and it's really relaxing. What about you? Did you see the new space film?
Yes, on Friday. It was so boring! I nearly fell asleep.
Really? My sister said it was frightening.
It wasn't frightening enough for me. And it was too long. Three hours!
I know. I was really disappointed. Next time I'll try a photography course!
Good idea! I'm very keen on it now. I'm going again next month.

questions.q: How did Priya feel at the start of the course?
questions.why: Priya says: I was nervous at first.

questions.q: What was the problem with the camera?
questions.why: Priya says: The camera was quite confusing. It has too many buttons!

questions.q: Why didn't Kwame like the film?
questions.a: It was boring and too long.
questions.why: Kwame says: It was so boring! And it was too long.

phrases.use: Asking somebody to describe a film, a place or a course.
Saying something was very, very good.
Saying you did not like something at all. So makes it stronger.
Saying how you felt at the start.
Saying what you want to know more about.
Saying there was more than you wanted.
Answering news that is not as good as you hoped.

items.meaning: Hard to understand.
items.example: The new bus timetable is really confusing.

items.meaning: You feel this when you cannot understand something.
items.example: I was confused, so I asked my manager again.

items.meaning: It makes you afraid.
items.example: Driving on the motorway at night is frightening for me.

items.meaning: Afraid.
items.example: She was frightened when the lights went out.

items.meaning: Sad, because something was not as good as you hoped.
items.example: I was disappointed when I didn't get the job.

items.meaning: Not as good as you hoped.
items.example: The hotel was disappointing. The room was small and dirty.

items.meaning: It makes you feel silly in front of other people.
items.example: I called my new manager by the wrong name. It was so embarrassing!

items.meaning: You feel this when you do something silly in front of people.
items.example: My phone rang in the meeting, and I was really embarrassed.

items.meaning: It helps you rest and feel less worried.
items.example: A walk by the river is very relaxing after work.

items.meaning: Very, very good. It surprises you.
items.example: The view from the top of the hill was amazing.

items.meaning: A bit afraid before something happens.
items.example: I'm always nervous before a job interview.

items.meaning: Wanting to do something very much. Keen on means you like it a lot.
items.example: Samir is very keen on cooking. He makes dinner every night.

items.meaning: Wanting to know about something.
items.example: I'm curious about the new café. Shall we try it?

items.meaning: Wanting to say thank you, because somebody helped you.
items.example: I'm very grateful for your help with the report.

sound.title: One strong part in long words
sound.explain: Long words have one strong part. Say it louder and longer. In interested and interesting, the strong part is IN. In disappointed, it is POINT. In embarrassed, it is BARR. The -ing word and the -ed word have the same strong part. Listen, then say each group.

sayIt.instructions: Say these lines from the conversation. Record yourself, then listen back. Can you hear the strong part in each long word?
lines: It was amazing. I was nervous at first, but everybody was very friendly.
The camera was quite confusing. It has too many buttons!
I'm interested in photography too. Is the course good for beginners?
It wasn't frightening enough for me. And it was too long. Three hours!

spot.instructions: Look at these sentences from the conversation. Some describe a thing. Some say how a person feels. Some say how much.
spot.question: Which words describe a thing? Which say how a person feels? Which words say how much? What small word comes after interested?
spot.answer: The -ing words describe the thing: boring, disappointing, confusing. The -ed words say how a person feels: disappointed, interested. Quite and too say how much. After interested comes in: interested in photography.

rules.title: boring or bored · good at, interested in, afraid of
rule: -ing tells you about the thing: The film was boring. The form is confusing.
-ed tells you how a person feels: I was bored. I'm confused.
The thing makes the feeling: The film was boring, so I was bored.
Some words have a small word after them: good at, interested in, afraid of.
More: keen on, nervous about, grateful for, curious about.
rules.mistake: Not: I'm interesting in photography. Say: I'm interested in photography.

rules.title: quite, too, not … enough
rule: quite = a good amount, but not very: The course was quite hard.
too + adjective = more than you want. It is a problem: It was too long.
not + adjective + enough = less than you need: It wasn't big enough.
You can count it: too many buttons. You can't count it: too much noise.
too + adjective + to + a verb: It's too cold to sit outside.
rules.mistake: Not: The course was too good! Say: The course was very good. Too means there is a problem.

practice.q: The film was so ___ . I nearly fell asleep.
practice.why: -ing tells you about the thing: the film was boring.

practice.q: I didn't understand the instructions. I was really ___ .
practice.why: -ed says how a person feels: I was confused.

practice.q: The news about the job was ___ . I didn't get it.
practice.why: -ing tells you about the thing: the news was disappointing.
Interested always has in after it.

practice.q: Tomasz is very good ___ fixing things.
practice.why: Good always has at after it: good at.
Afraid always has of after it: afraid of.

practice.q: The course was ___ good, but some parts were hard.
practice.why: Quite good means good, but not very good.

practice.q: I can't drink this coffee. It's ___ hot.
practice.why: Too hot is a problem: you can't drink it.

practice.q: The room wasn't big ___ for thirty people.
practice.why: not + adjective + enough: not big enough.

practice.q: I called my manager by the wrong name. I was so ___ !
practice.why: -ed says how a person feels: I was embarrassed.

yourTurn.prompt: Think of a place, a film or a course. Write four sentences. Say what it was like and how you felt. Use an -ing word, an -ed word, and too or not … enough.
yourTurn.model: Last month I went to a cooking class. It was amazing, and I was never bored. The kitchen was too small for twelve people. But I'm really interested in Thai food now.

text.title: A library notice board, and two references
text.body:
PRACTICE NOTICE: this library does not exist

HILLSIDE LIBRARY: NOTICE BOARD

FREE SATURDAY SESSIONS: MAKE IT AND MEND IT
10:00 Wood: bring an old chair or a small box.
12:00 Clothes: bring a shirt or a jacket with a hole.
Each session is one hour. Book at the front desk.

WHAT PEOPLE SAID
“I was nervous at first, but everybody was kind. It was worth it!” Lena
“The clothes session was interesting, but one hour isn't enough.” Samir

VOLUNTEERS WANTED
Can you help on Saturdays? Please bring a reference from an employer.

- - - - - - - -

PRACTICE REFERENCES: these people and companies do not exist

REFERENCE A
From: Carlos Ruiz, Manager, Brightway Supermarket
Omar Haddad worked with us for three years. He is honest and very reliable. He is never late, and he stays calm when the shop is busy. He is generous with his time, and he often helps new staff. He is the most hard-working person in my team. I recommend him.

- - - - - - - -

REFERENCE B
From: City Parcels
Omar Haddad worked here from May to October 2024. His work was OK. He did the tasks we gave him.

gist.q: What is on the library notice board?
gist.a: free sessions, and a request for volunteers
gist.why: The board shows the Saturday sessions, and it says: Volunteers wanted.
Reference A gives lots of good details, and it says: I recommend him.

detail.why: The notice says: Each session is one hour.

detail.q: What does Samir think of the clothes session?
detail.a: It was interesting, but too short.
detail.why: Samir says it was interesting, but one hour isn't enough.
The notice says: Please bring a reference from an employer.

detail.q: In Reference A, what is Omar like when the shop is busy?
detail.why: Reference A says: He stays calm when the shop is busy.

items.meaning: A letter from a person who knows you, often an old employer. It says what you are like at work.
items.example: My last manager wrote me a very good reference.

items.meaning: You can trust this person to do what they say, every time.
items.example: Ana is very reliable. She is never late.

items.meaning: Telling the truth.
items.example: He was honest and told his manager about the mistake.

items.meaning: Not worried, angry or excited.
items.example: Stay calm and call the office.

items.meaning: Happy to give time, help or money to other people.
items.example: My neighbour is very generous. She often cooks for me.

items.meaning: Working a lot, and always doing your best.
items.example: Our new cleaner is very hard-working.

items.meaning: A short text. It says what you think of a film, a book or a place.
items.example: I read the reviews before I booked the hotel.

items.meaning: To tell people that something or somebody is good.
items.example: Can you recommend a good dentist near here?

items.meaning: A time for one activity, like a class or a meeting.
items.example: The first training session is on Monday at ten.

items.meaning: Good enough for the money or the time you spend on it.
items.example: The course was expensive, but it was worth it.

model.title: A short review
model.body:
Saturday cooking class, Hillside Library: 4 out of 5
I went to the Saturday cooking class last month.
I was nervous at first, but the teacher was calm and kind.
The recipes were quite easy, and the food was amazing.
The kitchen was too small for twelve people, so it was a bit crowded.
It was free, and it was worth it. I recommend it to anybody who is interested in cooking.

write.task: Write a short review of a film, a course, a café or a day out. It can be real or made up. Say what it was like and how you felt. Then say if you recommend it.
checklist: I said what it was like, with an -ing word: amazing, boring …
I said how I felt, with an -ed word: bored, disappointed …
I used quite, too or not … enough once.
I said if I recommend it, and why.

card.title: Would you recommend it?
card.situation: Your colleague Mei wants to do something nice at the weekend. She asks about a film, a course or a day out that you went to.
card.goal: Tell Mei what it was like and how you felt. Say one good thing and one problem. Then say if you recommend it.

phrases: It was amazing. / It was quite good. / It was really disappointing.
I was nervous at first, but …
The only problem was … It was too …
I really recommend it. It's worth it.
prepare.notes: Choose a film, a course or a day out. Make notes. What was it like? How did you feel? Write one good thing and one problem. Do you recommend it?

doIt.liveClass: In the live class, your teacher is Mei. Tell her about your film, course or day out, and say if you recommend it. Then listen to another learner and ask: What was it like?
doIt.wehel: You are my colleague Mei. You want something to do at the weekend. Ask me about a film, a course or a day out. Ask: What was it like? How did you feel? Do you recommend it? Use simple English.

model.title: Mei asks about a day out
lines: Hi! I want to do something nice this weekend. Any ideas?
Well, I went to the Riverside Gardens on Sunday.
Oh, I'm curious about that place. What was it like?
It was amazing. The flowers were beautiful, and it was very relaxing.
Quite busy. The café was too crowded, so we had a picnic.
Tickets are £8. It isn't cheap, but it's worth it.
What can you do there if it rains?
There's a big glass house full of plants. You won't be bored.
Great. So do you recommend it?
Yes, I really recommend it. Go early, before it gets crowded.
compare: Did you say what it was like, with an -ing word?
Did you say how you felt, with an -ed word?
Did you say one good thing and one problem?
Did you say if you recommend it, and why?

canDo: I can say what something was like: amazing, boring, disappointing.
I can say how I felt: bored, confused, nervous.
I can use quite, too and not … enough.
I can read a notice board and two references.
I can review something and say if I recommend it.

reading.before: Look at the title and the first picture. How do the people feel? Why do you think they feel that way?
reading.talk: How did the people in the story feel at the start, and at the end? Would you recommend the story? Write two or three sentences, or say them to Wehel.

quiz.q: The meeting was three hours long. Everybody was ___ .
quiz.why: -ed says how people feel: everybody was bored.
Interested always has in after it.

quiz.q: The instructions were ___ . Nobody understood them.
quiz.why: -ing tells you about the thing: the instructions were confusing.

quiz.q: It's ___ cold to sit in the garden. Let's go inside.
quiz.why: too + adjective + to + a verb: too cold to sit outside.

quiz.q: The hall isn't big ___ for the party.
quiz.why: not + adjective + enough: not big enough.

quiz.q: A person who always does what they say is ___ .
quiz.why: You can trust a reliable person, every time.

quiz.q: The course was expensive, but it was ___ it.
quiz.why: It was worth it: good enough for the money.

quiz.q: I ___ TV when the lights went out.
quiz.why: The longer action, going on at the time: was watching.

quiz.q: We've only got ___ milk. Can you buy some?
quiz.why: You can't count milk, so use a little.
2021 is the start, so use since.

liveClass: Day 1: practise the Monday morning conversation in pairs. Then change the weekend: a concert, a match, a day at the sea. Listen for the -ing and -ed words.

Day 2: a feelings round. Each learner says a thing and a feeling: The traffic was frightening, so I was frightened. Then do a round of quite, too and not … enough about the room, the weather and the week.
Day 3: the task. You are Mei. Each learner reviews a film, a course or a day out and says if they recommend it. The others ask: What was it like?
Day 4: talk about the book, answer questions, and read two learners' reviews aloud.
